story: This Hubble image looks into Omega Centauri, which is both the biggest and the brightest of the sky's globular clusters. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars held together by gravity, and Omega Centauri has long posed puzzles for astronomers.

A discovery has now resolved part of that mystery. Images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, together with measurements from the GMOS spectrograph at Chile's Gemini South telescope, suggest that the cluster seems to hide a hard-to-find intermediate-mass black hole in its core.

Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to bridge the gap between the black holes left by single stars and the supermassive ones found at the hearts of large galaxies. They have proved hard to find, which is why a candidate in a cluster within our own galaxy attracts attention. Like any black hole, it cannot be seen directly. Its presence has to be inferred from its effect on its surroundings.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (9.97 x 9.09 arcminutes) and distance (17000 light years), the frame spans roughly 49 × 45 light-years. Its light set out about 17,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue and red filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view separates individual stars in the crowded cluster, while the black hole itself is invisible and can only be detected through its influence.

explore: Omega Centauri lies about 17,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Centaurus, and it is also cataloged as NGC 5139. The black hole result drew on two very different instruments, a camera in space and a spectrograph on the ground.
